6.0.0.en: 1 And do not become an enemy after having been a friend, for the one of evil repute inherits shame and disgrace, and so does the sinner who has a double tongue. 2 Do not be like a bull, exalting yourself in the thoughts of your heart, lest your soul be plundered, 3 and you eat up your leaves, and destroy your fruits, and leave yourself like dry wood. 4 The wicked soul destroys its owner, and makes him a derision to his enemies.

6.0.1.en: Ben Sirach looks to God's love for His creation, for He has granted nearly every living creature to love its like by natural instinct (Sir 13:14-15). As for human beings, He gave them the possibility of establishing friendship among themselves in full freedom, through the gifts God gave them of mind, emotion and the instincts of love. But since man declined by his fall into sin, he came to suffer need of a faithful, sincere friendship, which it is hard to find as he desires it even in those nearest to him. The child complains: "No one feels for me and understands me. My parents do not understand me."

6.0.2.en: Under the natural law, Job felt deprived of the faithful friendship that would support him in his affliction. His sons died and left him without help, and his wife, instead of supporting him, said to him: "Curse (bless) the Lord and die" (Job 2:9), and his friends came to comfort him, but heaped hurtful accusations upon him. Job cried out: "Miserable comforters are ye all" (Job 16:2).

6.0.3.en: And under the Law of Moses the psalmist cried out: "I said in my haste, All men are liars" (Ps 116:11). Jesse neglected his young son David, and did not present him to the prophet Samuel when he asked him to call his sons (1 Sam 16:11), and King Saul disregarded all David's effort to rescue him, his army and his people from the enemy, repaid him evil for good, and devoted his energies and resources to killing him (1 Sam 19:1). Absalom rebelled against David his father and wanted to kill him (2 Sam 16:11). The prophet complained, saying: "When my father and my mother forsake me, then the Lord will take me up" (Ps 27:10).

6.0.4.en: And in the New Testament, Luke the Evangelist understood the need of all humanity for a faithful friend, and so he presented the Lord Christ as the friend of all humanity, and therefore often called Him "the Son of man". The Evangelist proclaimed this Friend who in His friendship toward humanity did not single out a particular people, but is the lover of mankind, who "seeketh that which was lost" (Lk 19:10). And in the Lord Christ's parables He mentioned the lost sheep, the lost coin and the prodigal son without specifying any particular nationality or people. This Friend did not disdain meeting the sinful woman (Lk 7:26-35), Zacchaeus the tax collector (Lk 19:1-10) and the crucified thief (Lk 23:40-43). He also took care to meet children, women and the needy, and did not disdain touching the leper. He came to us as a friend, to satisfy the emotion of love, so that we may accept His friendship and befriend Him. He came to us as a divine friend, through whom we befriend people and accept their friendship. And as the perfect friend, in Him we understand friendship, taste it and practice it.

6.0.5.en: v Imagine a circle from whose center rays or lines go out. The farther the lines are from the center, the farther they are from one another... And conversely, the nearer they come to the center, the nearer they come to one another.

6.0.6.en: Suppose that this circle is the world, and the center of the circle is God. And the lines from the circumference to the center are the way of life of human beings; we find the same thing: the more the saints move inside the circle toward the center, desiring to draw near to God, the more they draw near to one another[1].

6.1.0.en: St. Dorotheus: v There is no true love with which we love others unless we love God. Every person loves his neighbor as himself if he is a lover of God, but if he does not love God he does not love himself[2].

6.2.0.en: v Let us train ourselves in love for the brethren... for if you love your brother you will behold God, because by your love for your brother you behold the very Love in whom God dwells[3].

6.2.1.en: St. Augustine: Man longs to find a faithful friend, and to be himself a sincere friend, if possible to all. What, then, are the marks of the faithful friend in whom we may rest assured, and what is it fitting for us to be marked by in order to be faithful friends?

6.2.2.en: A. Steadfastness in friendship. B. Not haughty. C. Like a tree ever leafy and fruitful. D. Holy. E. Sweet of tongue. F. Has passed the test of friendship. G. Friendship is not based on private benefit. H. Friendship is not based on courtesies and banquets. I. Friendship does not overstep fitting bounds. J. Caution about friends.

6.3.0.en: Do not turn from a friend into an enemy, for a bad reputation brings shame and disgrace; so it is with the sinner who has a double tongue [1].

6.3.1.en: Ben Sirach calls the believer never to turn from a friend (philo) into an enemy, and not to accept as a friend one who does this to anyone. The cohesion of society rests on faithful friendship, which is necessary whether on a personal basis or a collective trust. Some see that the word "enemy" here originally means one who is arrogant, so that no one trusts him, who is unable to deal with others in a spirit of friendship, who is accustomed to backbiting, who avoids tenderness and is quick to quarrel. These traits apply to the one the Holy Bible calls the fool. He who abides in God, the friend of mankind, abides in friendship and love, if possible, toward all people, without wavering in his love, and so is not a fool.

6.4.0.en: It is fitting that we not enter into friendship with a haughty person, and that we ourselves not be haughty.

6.4.1.en: Do not exalt yourself by the counsel of your own soul, lest your soul be torn to pieces as by a bull [2].

6.4.2.en: In his folly a man exalts himself over others, counting himself loftier than everyone he meets, while the genuine friend desires his friend to be better than himself and to have more success, joy and happiness.

6.4.3.en: In the ancient agricultural societies, fences were few, and young bulls would leave their pasture to seek food and grass, and big strong bulls would confront them, and might attack them and tear them to pieces. Therefore it is fitting for the believer to shelter within a strong wall, and not to think that he is the guide of his own spiritual life, and so not seek the counsel of a spiritual father who supports him in the Lord and keeps him from the blows of the enemy.

6.5.s.en: C. Like a tree ever leafy and fruitful:

6.5.0.en: Then you will devour your leaves, and destroy your fruits, and leave yourself like a dry tree [3].

6.5.1.en: It is fitting for the friend to be planted by the streams of the waters of the Holy Spirit (Ps 1), practicing a life of constant reliance on God with joy, and for God to be everything to him.

6.6.0.en: Let us flee from evil, lest our wicked souls perish and our friends perish. Just as the Holy Bible called us to walk in holiness and cleave to holy friends, at the same time it warns us against association with wicked friends. And the Fathers spoke at length of friendship with the wicked because of its danger; I quote a little of it, and the subject of friendship has already been treated at some length[4].

6.6.1.en: v Sitting with those who are not wise breaks up the heart, and conversation with the virtuous is a sweet spring.

6.6.2.en: v Do not stoop to the slack, or you will bring yourself down to the lower rank; rather let your converse be with the lovers of good, that your dwelling with them may be in the heights. Therefore let your abode be boldly in the places where the higher knowledge is. Go to the city of light and do not stoop to sinners.

6.6.3.en: Mar Isaac the Syrian: v "Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners" (1 Cor 10:33)... You despise gold; another loves gold.

6.6.4.en: You reject wealth; he seeks wealth with passion.

6.6.5.en: You love silence, weakness and the private life, while he finds his happiness in vain talk without restraint in the public square and the streets and the shops of drugs...

6.6.6.en: Do not remain with him under one roof. Do not rely on your former chastity. For you cannot be holier than David or wiser than Solomon...

6.6.7.en: If your role in the priestly work is to visit a widow or a virgin, do not enter the house alone. Let people who will not give offense accompany you...

6.7.0.en: Do not sit alone with a lady in secret without witnesses. If she has a secret matter that she wants to disclose, there must be with her a nurse, or a virgin, or a widow, or a married woman. She cannot pour out her secrets to you without a woman friend of hers being present[5].

6.8.0.en: v Do you not see that "evil communications corrupt good manners"? By them you cannot utter the Gospel, but only hear the words of idols. By them you lose the truth that Christ is God, and what you drink there you vomit up in the Church[6].

6.8.1.en: St. Augustine: v A young man who keeps a young man company in evil, let those who discern weep over them both.

6.8.2.en: v O lover of God, when you see hypocrites trading words of deceit and fraud, flee from there, lest their deadly words cling to your ears.

6.8.3.en: v These are the fuel of Satan who wrestles with us, which kindle the fire that burns us: corrupt talk with the laity... and the mother of evils is the throat and the company of idle brethren. If our souls are stripped of this burning fuel, they do not fall into the snares of our adversaries, and swiftly can fly to God, and through Him be delivered from the plots of the devil.

6.8.4.en: The friendship of companions in idleness and amusement fills you with gluttony and evil.

6.8.5.en: Ah, what is this unclean love and defiled deed?! Flee, my brother, from those accustomed to this. Do not eat with them and do not befriend them. Their table is unclean, and demons are helpers in preparing it; the lovers of the Bridegroom Christ do not taste it.

6.8.6.en: The banquet of the gluttonous man, distracted with delicacies... defiles the soul of the meek, while a dry crust of bread from the table of the pure of soul cleanses it of all pains and defilements.

6.8.7.en: The smell of the table of evil corrupts the intention of the pure, and the child is drawn to it like a dog to the butcher's house. But the table of him who persists at all times in prayer surpasses the fragrance of musk, and he who is a lover of God longs for it as for a treasure.

6.8.8.en: The spiritual elder: v If you take for yourself a faithful friend and he receives you to himself, then if you are weak he strengthens you and makes you courageous. He makes you a laborer and a striver, and becomes for you a solid fence and a strong support that helps you, and is for you like a shading tree where you rest from all your labors. And he is for you strength, steadfastness and consolation in your affliction, and you find him in your hardships bearing all your burdens. And if you cast all your burdens upon him, he lifts them from you.

6.8.9.en: St. Anba Paula of Tamwah: v If you are unable to be rich in God, cleave to him who is rich in Him, that you may be made happy by his happiness, and learn how to walk according to the commandments of the Gospel.

6.8.10.en: St. Pachomius: v If you have a friendship with one of the brethren and harm comes to you because of your association with him, hasten and cut yourself off from him. I do not say this to you, beloved, so that you may hate people, no, but so that you may cut off the causes of vice.

6.8.11.en: St. Ephrem the Syrian: v Hear what the Lord says: "Wherefore if thy hand or thy foot offend thee, cut them off, and cast them from thee: it is better for thee to enter into life halt or maimed, rather than having two hands or two feet to be cast into everlasting fire. And if thine eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee: it is better for thee to enter into life with one eye, rather than having two eyes to be cast into hell fire" (Mt 18:8-9). He did not say that about the members, but about brethren, and for the sake of relatives who hold with us the place of necessary members... So He says that nothing is more harmful than evil company and wicked fellowship, for friendship many times harms or benefits... So He commands us with great plainness to cut off those who harm us...

6.8.12.en: He was not content with pronouncing woe on him through whom offenses come, but showed us the way by which a person is saved from offenses. What is this way? He said: Cut off the friendship of the wicked... so that you do not gain them and lose your own soul along with them.

6.8.13.en: v If evil communications corrupt good manners, as the Apostle says, then we ought always to flee from association with the wicked and the scoffers and their like. For mingling with them and hearing their talk draws the simple-hearted to take on their ways.

6.8.14.en: St. John Chrysostom: The wicked soul destroys its owner, and makes him an object of malicious mockery among his enemies [4].

6.8.15.en: Our holy Christ asks in His farewell prayer: "And for their sakes I sanctify myself, that they also might be sanctified through the truth" (Jn 17:19). It is fitting for the believer not only to be sanctified by the Lord, but also to ask on behalf of all humanity, as his friends, that they be sanctified in the truth, so that he may enjoy friendship with them even in heaven forever.

6.9.0.en: For every morning he sings: "Set a watch, O Lord, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips" (Ps 141). Through this divine guard his tongue becomes sweet, drawing many to constructive friendship. Though we may have holy friends numbering a thousand, there is no friend who occupies the whole heart, mind and feelings, and leads our depths, our words and our conduct, except the one Friend, the Lord of glory Jesus.

6.10.0.en: 5 A sweet mouth multiplies friends, and a gentle tongue multiplies kindly greetings. 6 Let those who are at peace with you be many, but your counselors one of a thousand. 7 If you acquire a friend, acquire him after testing, and do not trust him quickly. 8 For there is a friend in his own day, but he does not abide in the day of your distress. 9 And there is a friend who becomes an enemy, and he will disclose the disgrace of your quarrel. 10 And there is a friend who shares your table, but he does not abide in the day of your distress. 11 He will be as yourself in your wealth, and will make himself bold among your household, 12 but if you are brought low, he will be against you, and will hide himself from your face. 13 Keep away from your enemies, and beware of your friends.

6.10.1.en: Sweet speech multiplies his friends, and a gentle tongue multiplies kindly greetings [5].

6.10.2.en: The true friend, unlike the fool, has sweet speech, and it is easy to approach him, as it is easy for him to approach others. Sweet speech full of love and gentleness is a treasure for forming successful friendships. On the contrary, negative talk, such as coarse joking, mockery and harsh words, shatters friendship and turns it into enmity. Who are the friends whom the sweet voice of the Crucified drew, if not the believers from all the nations? And who are the venerable ones, if not the heavenly orders who rejoice in our salvation? A good word prepares the way for friendship [6:5], while rude talk spoils friendship (Prov 16:21; 22:11).

6.11.s.en: F. Has passed the test of friendship [7]:

6.11.0.en: It is fitting for a person to examine the genuineness of friendship (Mt 7:16), by assessing the friend's conduct in time of distress. It is clear that Ben Sirach suffered from his former friends, and God Himself rescued him (51:2-3).

6.12.0.en: Let those who are at peace with you be many, and your counselors one of a thousand [6].

6.12.1.en: The ideal, supreme friendship is that which the Lord Christ proclaimed concerning Himself, for He died in the body to give them fellowship with Him in His life and His glories. Thus our Christ opened the door of friendship to humanity through the Cross; and the wonder is that those who crucified Him, the sons of men, heard Him say: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do" (Lk 23:34).

6.12.2.en: v Do not take for yourself many friends, and you will remain in rest all the days of your life.. for it is written: If your affairs are many you will not escape sin. "Let your counselor be one of a thousand" (cf. Sir 6:6), and also: "A faithful friend is the medicine of life" (Sir 6:16), likewise: "A faithful friend, his goodness has no balance. A faithful friend, nothing equals him" (cf. Sir 6:15).

6.13.0.en: St. Anba Paula of Tamwah: If you take a friend, take him after testing, and do not trust him quickly [7].

6.13.1.en: A person usually takes heed of the enemy's actions, but he must also beware of the unexpected actions of the friend. The Evangelist John says: "But Jesus did not commit himself unto them, because he knew all men, and needed not that any should testify of man: for he knew what was in man" (Jn 2:24-25).

6.14.s.en: G. Friendship is not based on private benefit:

6.14.0.en: For there is a friend for the sake of his own benefit, but he does not stay beside you in the day of your distress [8].

6.14.1.en: Ben Sirach warns us against friendship for personal benefit, instead of openness toward others, especially in times of affliction. There are friendships even among sinners and criminals for the sake of a shared evil benefit.

6.15.0.en: And there is a friend who may turn into an enemy, and so declares war on your faults [9].

6.15.1.en: Unfaithful friendship, for one reason or another, turns into enmity, exploiting the weaknesses of friends in order to expose them. Ben Sirach expresses what goes through the minds of many in every age, namely the fears of temporary friendships, especially those that turn into enmity! Therefore he recorded for us the negative sides as well as the positive, that we may enjoy true friendships with the incarnate Word of God and with our brethren in humanity.

6.16.s.en: H. Friendship is not based on courtesies and banquets:

6.16.0.en: And there is a friend who sits with you at the table, but does not stand beside you in the day of your distress [10].

6.16.1.en: Among the friendships without true roots are those based on courtesies and banquets without support in time of affliction. Courtesies and banquets, especially exaggerated ones, embarrass friends who are unable to keep pace with such conduct because of the exaggerated cost. Friendship has many levels. There are friendships on a seasonal level, such as the school friend; when a person graduates from his university, his friendship with his schoolmates disappears. And there are friendships between children that may last for a lifetime, even if there are long distances between the friends' residences. And there are friendships that are broken off by involuntary circumstances, but a person remains faithful to his friend even if he no longer sees him, even after death, like the friendship of David and Jonathan the son of Saul (1 Sam 20:13-15); David remained faithful to his promise to his friend even after his friend's death.

6.16.2.en: v Do you not know who is the unfaithful friend who sits at the table? He is Judas himself, who betrayed the Master with a kiss, became a hypocrite by his traitorous kiss, and became a type of the people of whom it was said: "This people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me" (cf. Isa 29:13)[7].

6.16.3.en: St. Clement of Alexandria: v How does the friend differ from the flatterer? The flatterer speaks to give pleasure, while the friend does not hold back from anything even if there is pain in it.

6.16.4.en: St. Basil the Great: v Nothing establishes love so strongly as sharing in joy and sorrow. Because you are far from troubles, do not isolate yourself from sharing with others also. When your neighbor is troubled, count the affliction as your own. Share his tears so as to support his crushed spirit, and share his joy so that the joy in him may become deep and rooted.

6.16.5.en: Establish love, for in this you serve yourself more than you serve him. For by your tears you become compassionate, and by the feelings of gladness you cleanse yourself of envy and gloom... If you cannot remove evils from him, share with him by your tears, and you remove half of the evil from him; and if you cannot increase his good things, share his joy, and you add something great to him[8].

6.17.s.en: I. Friendship does not overstep fitting bounds:

6.17.0.en: He rejects friendships that do not keep to fitting bounds, such as a person's dealing with the friend's family and servants with excessive boldness, relying on his friend's trust in him.

6.18.0.en: In your success he is like yourself, and speaks boldly to your servants [11].

6.19.0.en: But if you are brought low, he turns against you, and hides himself from your face [12].

6.19.1.en: The faithful friend remains sincere in the days of his gladness as in the days of distress.

6.20.0.en: So with the widening of the heart in love for friends and trust in them, Ben Sirach warns us not to allow ourselves to break a divine commandment or ignore it for the sake of our friendship with anyone.

6.21.0.en: Keep away from your enemies, and beware of your friends [13].

6.22.s.en: 3. Who is the unique faithful friend?

6.22.0.en: 14 A faithful friend is a strong defence, and he who has found one has found a treasure. 15 A faithful friend has no equal, and his goodness has no balance. 16 A faithful friend is the medicine of life, and those who fear the Lord will find him. 17 He who fears the Lord will obtain good friendship, for his friend will be like himself.

6.22.1.en: After speaking of the negative sides of unfaithful friendship (6:8-13), he spoke of the faithful friend (6:14-17), who is a treasure beyond price. Here he speaks of the unique friendship with the Heavenly One!

6.22.2.en: The believer finds in Christ Jesus a unique friend; when he is united with Him by the work of the Holy Spirit he enjoys participation in the divine nature (2 Pet 1:4). In this he enjoys the work of His traits in him, and becomes fit to establish friendship with many.

6.22.4.en: A. A strong refuge [14]: We defy the powers of the devil, whom the Lord crushes under our feet. So our friends see in us people of God kept in Him, and we pray for them that they may taste in us the work of the Savior who delivers from evil.

6.22.5.en: B. A precious treasure [14]: He who possesses him feels no need or want. For our Christ is our treasure. And in Christ Jesus we offer them what is Christ's, so that they are satisfied and refreshed, not from us, but from Him who works in us and in them!

6.23.0.en: C. Nothing equals him [15]: In Christ the Lord turns our hearts into a new heaven, and declares His Kingdom in us according to His true promise (Lk 17:21). In our friendship with our beloved, we enjoy His promise: "Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them" (Mt 18:20).

6.23.1.en: D. The medicine of life: For He is the physician of souls and bodies, who gives us His Body and Blood to partake of, so that we enjoy eternal life (Jn 6:52). As He is the Head of the Church, we share with our brethren who are spiritually sick, asking the Lord to reveal Himself to them as physician and medicine for their souls.

6.24.0.en: E. We shall not enjoy this heavenly Friend unless we walk in the fear of the Lord [17].

6.24.1.en: A faithful friend is a strong refuge, and he who has found one has found a treasure [14].

6.24.2.en: A faithful friend has no equal, and there is none who can weigh his loftiness [15].

6.24.3.en: After Ben Sirach revealed humanity's need for a faithful friend, warning us against friendships without true roots, and proclaiming the greatness of true friendships, now he lifts the veil from this friendship, namely union with divine Wisdom, through a sincere desire for continual learning, for the sake of which the Wisdom of God Himself became incarnate, that we may possess Him in us, and dwell in Him, and be glorified with Him forever.

6.24.4.en: v There is nothing in this world more precious than the faithful friend, and there is no balance that can weigh his loftiness.

6.24.5.en: A faithful friend is a firm refuge and a strong palace.

6.24.6.en: A faithful friend is the treasure of life.

6.24.7.en: A faithful friend is better than gold, and more precious than a precious stone.

6.24.8.en: A faithful friend is a garden enclosed and a spring shut up (Song 4:12), opened and enjoyed in its time.

6.24.9.en: A faithful friend is a refreshing harbor, surpassing all understanding; what a great grace![9]

6.24.10.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus: A faithful friend is the medicine of life, and those who fear the Lord will find him [16].

6.24.11.en: It is fitting for the believer to find in his friend the fear of the Lord, for this is the guarantee of true friendship between them; for he who is not a friend of the Lord cannot be trusted for friendship with him.

6.24.12.en: v "A faithful friend is the medicine of life" (Sir 6:16).

6.24.13.en: There is no remedy so effective in healing pains as the sincere friend who comforts you in your afflictions, manages you in your problems, rejoices in your success and grieves in your calamities. He who has found such a friend has found a treasure. For the faithful friend has no like, and the weight of gold and silver does not equal the goodness of his faithfulness (Sir 6:14-15).

6.24.14.en: v Truly, let you have a friend whom you call "half of my soul".

6.24.15.en: v There is no true friendship unless you make it like a joint that welds souls, so that they cleave together by the love poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit.

6.24.16.en: v There is no effective remedy for healing pains like the sincere friend who comforts you in your afflictions.

6.24.17.en: St. Augustine: He who fears the Lord directs his friendship well, for as he is, so is his neighbor [17].

6.24.18.en: v Man touches with his mind the indescribable divine power, and with his body he draws near to the animals. But few are those who are truly rational and who strive to direct their thoughts toward God the Redeemer and to enjoy kinship with Him, and to show this in their works and virtuous life. As for the majority, those whose spirits lack good sense, they disdain the immortal divine sonship, and incline toward the wretched, short-lived bodily kinship that will end one day, thinking only of what is of the flesh, burning with lust like the dumb animals, depriving their souls of God by their deeds, and descending in their spirits from heaven to the abyss of fleshly lusts[10].

6.24.19.en: St. Anthony the Great: He who carries the fear of the Lord in his heart, and walks in the spirit of godliness in the wisdom of the Spirit, obtains good friendship not only among human beings, but even with the heavenly orders such as the angels.

6.24.20.en: v The wealth of knowledge and wisdom brings many angels to us, while the corrupt person is cut off even from the angel who was given to him at his birth. Spiritual friendship is a virtue, and through the knowledge of God our souls are joined in friendship with the holy powers. So it is said that human beings who repent cause joy to the angels (Lk 15:10), since they become ready to receive greater wisdom. So also Abraham, rich in knowledge, offered a secret table to the friends who appeared to him at midday[11].

6.25.0.en: 18 My son, take discipline from your youth, and you will find wisdom until your old age. 19 Like the plowman and the sower, come to her, and wait for her good fruits. 20 For you will labor a little in tilling her, and will eat of her produce soon. 21 How hard she is to the undisciplined! The one who lacks understanding will not continue with her, 22 for she is to him like a heavy testing stone; and he will not be long in casting her off. 23 For wisdom is according to her name, and she is not plain to many, but those who know her, she abides with them until the beholding of God. 24 Hear, my son, and receive my opinion, and do not cast away my counsel, 25 and put your feet into her fetters, and your neck into her yoke. 26 Bow your shoulder and carry her, and do not be vexed at her chains. 27 Come to her with all your soul, and keep her ways with all your might. 28 Search and seek, and she will be made known to you, and when you have obtained her, do not let her go. 29 For at the last you will find her rest, and she will be turned for you into gladness. 30 Then her fetters will be for you a strong protection, and her chains a robe of glory. 31 For on her is a golden ornament, and her chains are a cord of blue. 32 You will put her on as a robe of glory, and bind her on as a crown of rejoicing. 33 If you will, my son, you will be disciplined, and if you yield yourself, you will gain shrewdness. 34 If you love to hear, you will understand, and if you incline your ear, you will become wise. 35 Stand in the company of the elders, and cleave to him who is wise. Desire to hear every godly discourse, and do not neglect the proverbs of understanding. 36 And if you see a man of understanding, rise early to him, and let your foot wear the steps of his door. 37 Meditate on the ordinances of the Lord, and in His commandments ponder at all times; He will establish your heart, and will give you the wisdom you desire.

6.25.1.en: The way to enjoy friendship with Wisdom herself is:

6.25.2.en: A. Continual learning for the acquisition of wisdom [18-22].

6.27.0.en: C. Seeking her [26-28]. 1. She gives you rest [28]. 2. Strong protection [29]. 3. Splendid glory [29]. 4. Heavenly experience [30]. 5. Knowledge and shrewdness [32]. 6. Understanding and wisdom [33].

6.27.1.en: The word paideia occurs 28 times in the book of Proverbs in the Septuagint, and is often a translation of musar, that is, "instruction" or "training". In this book it occurs 36 times, and it has a deeper meaning than "learning".

6.27.2.en: A. It is fitting for the believer to be a lover of learning from his youth [18]. Disciples need to seek wisdom in their youth.

6.27.3.en: B. The way of wisdom is narrow and needs striving and patience; the striver is like a farmer who plows and sows and awaits the good harvest, so that he enjoys the joyful fruits [19]. Fools find patience and striving hard, and count that as heavy on their souls, while the wise man counts these toils as a matter of course (Prov 12:1; Heb 12:11).

6.27.4.en: C. We enjoy friendship with wisdom through being disciplined with a serious heart [20].

6.27.5.en: D. We do not fear trials all along the way; through them we pass over to glories [21-24].

6.27.6.en: E. As long as we are in the body we do not cease seeking wisdom and holding fast to her until the last breath [25-28].

6.28.0.en: F. Receiving wisdom as a heavenly bride and a rejoicing queen [29-31].

6.29.0.en: G. Growing in her through continual learning, benefiting from the experience of the devout elders, and enjoying the divine commandment [32-37].

6.29.1.en: My son, choose instruction from your youth, and you will find wisdom in your old age [18].

6.29.2.en: To enjoy wisdom, we need to care for the inner life, where a person comes to the stage of maturity after training in sanctifying the soul and controlling the passions, practicing the virtuous life, grasping the meaning of true tradition, studying God's law and seeking divine grace, so that the Lord grants him true wisdom. The person trains himself in this so as to enjoy mature wisdom in his old age. St. Augustine wrote to his son beloved in the Lord, Palatianus: [Your strong and fruitful dealings with the Lord our God have led us to great joy. You have chosen your instruction from your youth that you may find wisdom at your old age (Sir 6:18). For man's understanding is gray hair, and an unspotted life is old age (Wis 4:8-9) [12].]

6.29.3.en: v "Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? by taking heed thereto according to thy word" (cf. Ps 119:9)... Does the old man despair of this? Or does the old man amend his way by some means other than the word of God? Or is this counsel so that we may know in which age we must first of all amend our way, as it is written: "My son, gather instruction from thy youth up: so shalt thou find wisdom till thine old age" (cf. Sir 6:18)[13].

6.29.4.en: St. Augustine: v Almost all bodily graces change with time. Wisdom alone increases while all the other works (in man) fade. Fasting, sleeping on the ground, moving from one place to another, hospitality to travelers, defending the poor, persevering in standing in prayer, visiting the sick, working with the hands to bring money for almsgiving; all the works, in short, that the body practices decrease with its weakness[14].

6.29.5.en: St. Jerome: Come to her like the plowman and the sower, and wait for her good harvest, for you will labor a little in her work, and will eat of her fruit soon [19].

6.29.6.en: The believer's role is to strive in prayer, to accept discipline and to learn God's law, and so he plows and plants and cares for his heart and mind that his depths may become the Lord's field full of the fruit of wisdom. Just as the wise farmer does not seek the fruit at once, but prepares the ground and clears it of stones and thorns and plows it and sows and waters it, etc., and finally gathers the fruits, so it is fitting for him who seeks the fruit of wisdom to work. And it is fitting for him not to cease earnest work in acquiring wisdom and practicing it throughout his whole life, lest the ground of his heart turn into fallow and dry land through his negligence.

6.29.7.en: St. Ambrose says that there is only one who teaches and has no need to learn, namely God. As for us, whatever our position, age or culture, we remain in need of learning every day until the moment of our departure from this world.

6.29.8.en: v "Strive to enter in at the strait gate" (Lk 13:24)... The straight way is narrow, that is, any deviation from it is full of dangers, whether to the right or the left. It is like a bridge; whoever slips off it from either side falls into the river[15].

6.29.9.en: v "Return unto thy rest, O my soul; for the Lord hath dealt bountifully with thee" (Ps 116:7). The brave contender applies these altogether comforting words to himself, like Paul when he says: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith: henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness" (2 Tim 4:7-8). The prophet said this very thing to his own soul: "Since you complete sufficiently the way of this life, return to your rest, for the Lord has dealt bountifully with you." For eternal rest is set before those who strive in the present life, keeping the laws, a rest that is not a debt owed for our works, but from the grace of God, who is generous to those who hope in Him[16].

6.29.10.en: v He describes the future rest, comparing it with present things. He says: Here the sorrows of death have compassed me, but there He has delivered my soul from death. Here my eyes pour out tears because of troubles, but there no tear remains to dim the eyes of those who rejoice in contemplating the beauty of God's glory. For God wipes away all tears from all faces[17].

6.29.11.en: St. Basil the Great: v Basil the Great says: We cannot enjoy the pure Spirit while defilements are in our hearts; and also: love God without deceit, with all your souls and all your hearts and all your intentions, so that no doubt or suspicion may overtake your faith that God is the Helper. And also "pour out your hearts" means: give your effort and empty your aim for supplication and entreaty to God. Pouring means abundance and plenty, as the Apostle says that the love of God has been shed abroad in our hearts.

6.29.12.en: Father Anthimus of Jerusalem: She is hard to the undisciplined, and he who lacks a sound heart does not continue with her [20].

6.29.13.en: He warns us against haste in an unripe harvest, so it is fitting for the young man to enjoy the experience of those before him. To the ignorant and undisciplined, wisdom seems hard and requires effort and longing of heart for her, and he feels increasing and continual happiness, which turns his life into a perpetual paradise, so that he feels no boredom, but feels the delight of constant renewal.

6.29.14.en: So she is heavy for him like a testing stone, and he does not stay long before casting her off [21].

6.29.15.en: The young man who claims to have matured in wisdom is like one who collides with a heavy stone that shatters him. Perhaps Ben Sirach here refers to the many hardships he endured in order to obtain wisdom: prayer to ask wisdom from God, and journeys in the search for her, without being ashamed to seek her from young and old alike (cf. Sir 39:1-11).

6.29.16.en: For wisdom is worthy of her name, and is not made known to many [22].

6.29.17.en: Hear, my son, and receive my opinion, and do not cast away my counsel [23].

6.29.18.en: Put your feet into her fetters, and your neck into her collar [24].

6.29.19.en: The yoke of wisdom seems at first heavy fetters; he who submits to them by his own will and so controls himself finds the fetters turn into a sweet and easy yoke, as the Lord Christ said (Mt 11:29-30). The believer finds it a glorious robe and a mark of honor.

6.29.20.en: v It may also be understood that those who are shackled by the commandments of wisdom are bound, those for whom by patience the chains turn into ornaments, as it is written: "Put thy feet into her fetters" (cf. Sir 6:24)[18].

6.29.21.en: v It was said: "Put thy feet into the fetters" of wisdom, where wisdom is learned. He means the feet of the heart, not of the body; they are bound with her golden chains, so that he does not leave the way of God, and does not become a fugitive from it, and what we read we adopt, and the true meaning is kept safe[19].

6.29.22.en: v Many have kept their status as nobles, have kept their royal authority, and yet they are Christians. Such people are like those in fetters and bonds of iron. How so? They accepted the fetters to keep them from going to unlawful things; they accepted the fetters of wisdom, the fetters of the word of God.

6.29.23.en: Why are they fetters of iron and not of gold? They are iron as long as they fear. Let them love, and they become gold... The beginning is fetters of iron, and the end is a necklace of gold[20].

6.29.24.en: v The weakness and corruption of the body are truly fetters that weigh down the soul (Wis 9:15). The fragility of the body is like material used by a persecutor to cause pain and weariness; so (the weakness of the body) presses many saints toward evil. The Apostle longed to be freed from these fetters and to be with Christ, but to remain in the flesh was for the sake of necessity, for the benefit of those whom he served with the Gospel (Phil 1:23-24). Until this corruptible puts on incorruption and this mortal puts on immortality (1 Cor 15:53), the weak body imprisons the will of the Spirit (Mt 26:41; Mk 14:38). No one feels these fetters except those who groan within, who are burdened (2 Cor 5:3-4), and want to be clothed upon with the tabernacle which is from heaven, for death is terrifying and the dead life brings sorrow. The Apostle multiplied his groanings for the sake of the persons who suffer, so that their groanings may reach before the eyes of the Lord. Those who are bound with the disciplines of wisdom may also count these as fetters. But for him who endures these disciplines with patience, these fetters turn into ornaments, and so it was written: "Put thy feet into her fetters" [24][21].

6.29.25.en: St. Augustine: Bow your shoulder under her and carry her, and do not be angry at her fetters [25].

6.29.26.en: Come to her with all your soul, and keep her ways with all your might [26].

6.29.27.en: Acquiring wisdom requires of us self-control and giving up the natural inclinations of man, such as his unruly desire to talk and his desire also to dominate and get ahead of others and to boast; and therefore whoever wants to acquire wisdom must give up all of that. Perhaps at the beginning it is for him like a heavy yoke, which he must carry with joy and in silence, and it will not be long before he finds it light and joyful. And perhaps Ben Sirach had before him Joseph the righteous as a living example in this matter, being one of the wise men in the Holy Bible and in literature, in whom prophecy was joined with wisdom, and who did not obtain the two gifts except after testing and trial and a heavy yoke (Gen 37:28; Ps 105:16-22)[22].

6.29.28.en: v The wise must not listen to every kind of talk, but to what is useful, which leads to understanding the will of God. For His will is the way that brings people back again to life and eternal light[23].

6.29.29.en: St. Anthony the Great: Search and seek her, and she will become known to you, and when you have laid hold of her, do not let her go[24] [27].

6.29.30.en: v If for me "to live is Christ" (Phil 1:21), truly it is fitting that my words be about Christ, and all my thought and work depend on His commandments, and that my soul be shaped to be like Him[25].

6.29.31.en: St. Basil the Great: For at the last you will find her rest, and she will turn into gladness for you [28].

6.29.32.en: Then her fetters will be a strong protection for you, and her chains a robe of glory [29].

6.29.33.en: And her yoke will be an ornament of gold, and her fetters a cord of blue [30].

6.29.34.en: You will put her on as a robe of glory, and wear her as a crown of great rejoicing [31].

6.29.35.en: If you acquire wisdom she becomes a source of pride for you, and becomes like a crown that adorns the head, and necklaces that adorn the neck: "an ornament of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck" (Prov 1:9). For wisdom, represented whether in good speech or conduct, is a cause of delight both to the wise man and to those around him. Therefore kings, rulers and governors in many kingdoms surrounded themselves with the wise and the philosophers, adorning their councils, their courts and their palaces with them, and perhaps the manifestations of wisdom embodied here (strong protection, robe of glory, golden ornaments, purple garments, scarlet, crown of rejoicing) remind us of what Pharaoh of Egypt gave to Joseph: the ring, the garment, the fine linen and the gold chain (Gen 41:45). The blue cords in particular point to the Law. It is stated in the book of Numbers that the Israelites were bound to put a ribband of blue on the fringe of the borders of their garments, so that they might see it and remember all the commandments of the Lord and do them (Num 15:38-39). But here the devout see the fetters of wisdom as a golden ornament with a blue ribband, and they wear a robe of glory and carry a lofty crown (6:30-31). Truly heavenly wisdom makes of the believer a priest who offers the sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving (Rev 1:6), wearing a glorious robe (50:11) and a splendid crown (Prov 4:9)[26].

6.30.0.en: The requirements for acquiring wisdom are: A. The desire for continual learning [32].

6.31.0.en: B. The desire to listen [33] more than to speak. C. Cleaving to the wise who have experience [34].

6.32.0.en: D. Listening attentively to the divine commandment [35]. E. Earnestness and frequenting the places of the wise [36].

6.33.0.en: F. Sanctifying the mind at all times, which makes it steadfast, not shaken by every strange wind [37].

6.33.1.en: If you will, my son, you will learn, and if you give yourself, you will become shrewd [32].

6.33.2.en: Ben Sirach longs for the hearts of believers to be kindled with longing to learn wisdom, so that all may become wise.

6.33.3.en: If you love to listen you will acquire knowledge, and if you incline your ear you will become wise [33].
